content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Dengue fever cases are rising rapidly: Breaking the pattern of the epidemic season. The dengue fever epidemic is becoming increasingly complex, with a rapid increase in the number of cases, a widening distribution area, and unpredictable outbreak times. Worryingly, the disease is tending to occur year-round, no longer primarily concentrated in the rainy season as before. Báo Sài Gòn Giải phóng•10/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Increased number of patients with critical condition. The Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City recently admitted a 17-day-old boy (from Tan Vinh Loc commune) suffering from Dengue fever with multiple severe complications. Test results confirmed the child was infected with the Dengue virus, had a low platelet count, developed dengue shock, along with liver damage and blood clotting disorders, requiring intensive treatment. Medical staff at the City Children's Hospital examine and treat a child with severe dengue fever (PHOTO: Provided by the hospital). Previously, the hospital also treated a 27-month-old girl (from Thanh Hoa province) with dengue fever complicated by fulminant myocarditis, cardiogenic shock, and multiple organ failure. According to her medical history, the child had a continuous high fever for 3 days and vomited multiple times. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA The family bought unknown medications for the child to take on their own, only taking the child to the hospital when the child became lethargic. Just 12 hours after admission, the child developed respiratory failure, cyanosis, and a drop in blood pressure, requiring intubation, mechanical ventilation, and intensive care. At the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the number of severe dengue fever cases admitted is also rapidly increasing. Dr. Phan Vinh Tho, Head of Infectious Diseases Department D, said that the hospital is currently treating 14 severe cases, some of whom were admitted in a state of prolonged shock, multi-organ failure, and severe liver damage, requiring intensive resuscitation measures such as continuous hemodialysis, respiratory support, and blood product transfusions. Not only are severe cases appearing, but the number of dengue fever cases in Ho Chi Minh City is also increasing significantly. According to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), the city recorded 1,959 cases last week, a 16.2% increase compared to the average of the previous four weeks. Since the beginning of the year, the city has recorded a total of 44,549 cases. Areas with high dengue fever rates include Con Dao Special Zone, Ngai Giao commune, and Minh Thanh commune. Numerous changes in epidemiological characteristics. Faced with the reality of an increase in dengue fever cases, which is not following the usual seasonal pattern, the health sector has launched a high-intensity campaign to prevent and control the disease with the determination to bring the outbreak under control. You may also like Medical staff and the Dĩ An ward authorities provided guidance on how to address areas at risk of outbreaks. Dengue fever. Photo: THANH AN Dr. Huynh Minh Chin, Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Health, requested local authorities to mobilize forces for general environmental sanitation, thoroughly review and address risk areas, clearly assign responsibilities, and strengthen inspection and supervision. Each family should dedicate at least once a week to checking, rinsing, and covering water containers, removing waste materials that can collect water, and eliminating mosquito larvae; while also maintaining the habit of washing hands with soap, and cleaning children's toys and belongings to prevent dengue fever. According to MSc-Dr. Le Hong Nga, Deputy Director of HCDC, dengue fever is undergoing many changes in its epidemiological characteristics. Previously, the epidemic usually increased during the rainy season, with periods of significant decrease and outbreaks in large, cyclical waves. However, in recent years, the disease has tended to circulate year-round, with the number of cases remaining high and no longer following a distinct seasonal pattern as before. This is due to the impact of climate change, which alters temperature, rainfall, and humidity, creating favorable conditions for disease-transmitting mosquitoes to breed and develop. Furthermore, rapid urbanization, high population density, and the lack of regular cleaning of lodging houses, construction sites, and water containers create favorable environments for the breeding of Aedes mosquitoes. People who have previously had dengue fever can still be reinfected by a different type of the virus. The rotation of virus types, along with the development of insecticide-resistant mosquitoes, makes predicting and controlling outbreaks increasingly difficult. “There is currently no specific treatment for dengue fever. The disease typically progresses through a fever phase and a critical phase.” "Especially from the 3rd to the 7th day, when the patient's fever begins to subside, complications such as plasma leakage, shock, severe bleeding, or organ damage can still occur. Patients should not be complacent when the fever goes down; they need to closely monitor for warning signs and return for follow-up examinations as instructed," advised MSc-Dr. Le Hong Nga. According to the Ministry of Health , in the first 10 months of the year, the whole country recorded 170,684 cases and 21 deaths due to dengue fever. Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention, noted that dengue fever is not only occurring in high-risk areas in the South but is also spreading to mountainous provinces in the North such as Tuyen Quang and Son La - areas that previously recorded few cases. You may also like Changes in disease cycles, climate change, and the simultaneous circulation of multiple dengue virus strains are posing significant challenges to disease prevention and control efforts. The Dormitory and Urban Management Center of the Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City recently collaborated with the HCDC to organize a disease prevention and control awareness day at building E3, dormitory area B, to help students proactively prevent infectious diseases, especially dengue fever. According to Mr. Tran Van Dao, Vice Chairman of the People's Committee of Di An Ward, the locality has many lodging areas, residential areas interspersed with construction sites, vacant land, and areas at risk of breeding disease-carrying mosquitoes. From the beginning of the year until now, Di An Ward has recorded 794 dengue fever cases, 388 outbreaks, and one death. To proactively prevent dengue fever, the local authorities have mobilized forces to conduct comprehensive environmental sanitation, thoroughly address risk areas, and coordinate with the health sector to inspect and spray chemicals according to regulations. Daily Digest Following Photos Games Dengue second time: Doctor reveals why it can be more severe and shares warning signs to watch for If you have had dengue, you still need to take precaution against another infection. Having dengue once does not make you immune to all four types of the virus. Published on: Nov 9, 2026, 19:45:24 IST By Adrija Dey Prefer HTon Google Share via Copy link Dengue can be even more dangerous when it strikes a second time. This mosquito-borne viral infection causes fever, headaches, and body aches and can cause platelet counts to drop. Even after recovering from dengue, you need to continue taking precautions, as a previous infection does not protect against all types of viruses. Preventing mosquito bites and recognising warning signs are essential. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection. ALSO READ: Dengue or viral fever? Doctor explains why they may appear to be ‘similar’ and shares 9 signs to tell them apart Dr Harshad Limaye, director and senior consultant in infectious disease and internal medicine at Nanavati Max Super Speciality Hospital, Mumbai, discussed the possibility of getting dengue a second time. “A second infection can be more severe and in some cases, even life-threatening,” he said. Why can you get dengue again? Having dengue once does not give you complete immunity against the disease. Dr Limaye revealed that the dengue virus has four distinct serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. “While infection with one type induces protective immunity against that specific serotype, it does not confer long-term protection against the other three serotypes," he said. Since all four types have been reported in India, people who have recovered from one infection remain vulnerable to another caused by a different serotype. Why can a second infection be more severe? There is a substantial increase in getting dengue a second time, as it is linked to how antibodies from the first infection respond to a different type of dengue virus. He said, “During a second infection with a different type, the antibodies developed against the first type can attach to the virus, but they cannot destroy it. Instead, they help the virus enter immune cells more easily, increasing the viral load in the body. This is a unique process called antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE).” This means the immune response you developed from the previous infection can actually lead to more severe illness. But it is also important to note that a second infection does not automatically mean a person will develop severe dengue. Falling fever is not always a sign of recovery. (Picture credit: Pexel) How can severe dengue affect the body? Severe dengue can cause blood vessels to leak plasma, the liquid component of blood. Fluid may then accumulate around the lungs or in the abdominal cavity. Dr Limaye elaborated, “The immune system reaction causes the blood vessels to leak, leading to fluid accumulation in the lungs and abdominal cavity, which can progress to dengue shock syndrome (DSS). It is a severe condition in which plasma leakage causes circulatory failure, resulting in inadequate blood flow and oxygen delivery to vital organs.” Why does a falling fever not always mean recovery? Many associate a falling fever with recovery, but a drop in temperature does not mean the danger has passed. Dr Limaye cautioned that even after the fever subsides, one still needs to be cautious. Be alert to symptoms such as persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, bleeding from the gums or nose, marked fatigue or restlessness, reduced urination or signs of dehydration. Constant monitoring when the fever subsides is essential. The doctor warned that dengue is unpredictable and symptoms can worsen rapidly. How to reduce the risk of another infection? The expert's prevention advice includes removing stagnant water in and around homes, offices and schools, where dengue-carrying mosquitoes can breed. Similarly, construction sites need attention, as containers and uneven ground can collect water unnoticed. Proper drainage and regular checks can reduce these breeding sites. Alongside mosquito control measures, you should see a doctor immediately if you experience symptoms suggestive of dengue. content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue outbreak reaches 524 cases, here's where, how to avoid Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Nov. 6, 2026, 12:08 p.m. ET The historic surge in dengue fever continues. Florida reported 39 more locally acquired cases in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total for the year to 524 as of Oct. 31, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous record for Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases. The numbers may climb even higher in the weeks ahead after record rainfall left roads flooded, ditches full, and standing water in many Florida yards. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which has 407 confirmed cases. Locally acquired cases have now been reported in 12 counties. The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to issue a state of local emergency, which expires Nov. 12 unless the county extends it again as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever." One death has been confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. Florida's outbreak far exceeds the previous largest outbreak, which was 264 local cases in Hawaii's Big Island between September 2015 and March 2016. President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has been this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 20 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Sarasota Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas Seminole "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease-capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases continue to climb in Florida According to Florida Department of Health data released Nov. 6, 12 counties have reported 524 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 485 reported Oct. 24. There have also been eight positive samples of locally acquired West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 524 cases 407 in Hillsborough County 80 in Pinellas County 12 in Miami-Dade County 10 in Orange County 4 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: eight cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County ( incuding one asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? A local state of emergency in Hillsborough County expires Nov. 12. A state of local emergency can be in effect for only seven days, unless rescinded or extended, according to the Hillsborough County Department of Health. "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Trump wants mosquitoes, ticks eliminated in Washington, D.C. On Sept. 29, Trump signed an executive order to eliminate ticks and mosquitoes in Washington, D.C. The order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Administrator of General Services, along with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, to "develop and implement a campaign across Washington, D.C., to reduce invasive mosquito populations by 90 percent and the tick population by 50 percent by 2028 using safe and effective, non-chemical, and innovative technology-enabled methods. "This new model, localized to Washington, D.C., can later be applied nationwide as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. Cheryl McCloud and C. A. Bridges are journalists for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team. content: Advertisement Subscribe now Log in November 12, 2026 08:49 E-Paper E-Magazine Corporate CEO Talk Biz Link PR Newswire Media OutReach Newswire Investing M&A Outbound Investment Investing in Haiphong Your Consultant KPMG PwC Indochine Counsel Vilasia Ansarada Green Growth Energy Efficiency Rethinking Plastics BASF Property Green Buildings Industrial Properties Money Insurance Smart Payment Trends Stock Monitor Infographics Timeout Travel Hotels & Restaurants The Insider Entertainment Lifestyle Sports Photos Society Swing for the Kids CSR World News Society Swing for the Kids CSR Translating scientific evidence into practice for dengue control November 06, 2026 | 16:12 (0) user say Share Email Print More than 700 leading Vietnamese and international experts, policymakers, and businesses gathered at the Dengue Summit 2026 in Hanoi on November 5–6 to discuss the importance of shifting towards proactive prevention amid a growingly complex dengue landscape. The event was organised by the Vietnam Administration of Disease Prevention under the Ministry of Health (MoH), in collaboration with Hanoi Medical University (Centre for Training and Technology Transfer), the Centre for Community Health Research and Injury Prevention (CCHIP), Takeda Pharmaceuticals Vietnam, and other partner organisations. It was attended by representatives from the Ministry of Health, the World Health Organization (WHO), and Departments of Health and Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDCs) from 34 provinces and cities nationwide. The Dengue Summit 2026 in Hanoi. Photo: Thai Binh Held for the second consecutive year, the summit served as a forum for sharing the latest data, scientific evidence, and international experience in dengue treatment and prevention, helping translate scientific knowledge into practice in Vietnam. The summit featured four thematic sessions, more than 15 in-depth presentations, and more than 60 scientific research posters, covering epidemiology, clinical practice, communication, prevention, digital technology, and health policy. Dengue is one of the world's fastest-growing mosquito-borne infectious diseases, with an estimated 100-400 million infections annually. In Vietnam, dengue has remained persistent for more than four decades. Since 1980, the country has recorded hundreds of thousands of cases each year, with deaths reported annually. The dengue incidence rate per 100,000 people is significantly higher than that of other infectious diseases - ranking first in incidence and second in mortality among infectious diseases in Vietnam. In 2025, Vietnam recorded 184,903 cases - the highest in the Asia-Pacific region, surpassing the Philippines, Indonesia, and Bangladesh. In the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam recorded 170,684 dengue cases and 21 deaths. The disease circulates year-round across all provinces and cities, and is spreading to northern mountainous provinces such as Tuyen Quang and Son La – the areas that previously reported few cases. All four dengue virus serotypes are circulating in Vietnam, with dominant serotypes varying over time and by region. Cyclical shifts in circulating serotypes, combined with climate change, rapid urbanisation, and insecticide-resistant mosquito populations, have made dengue outbreaks increasingly difficult to predict. Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, director general of the Vietnam Administration of Disease Prevention. Photo: Thai Binh Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, director general of the Vietnam Administration of Disease Prevention, said, “Vietnam needs decisive, proactive, and evidence-based disease prevention strategies. At the same time, adapting relevant international experience to local conditions, alongside vector control and greater public awareness, is essential for improving prevention outcomes and reducing the burden.” During the plenary session, experts presented evidence showing how vaccination programmes have contributed to measurable progress in several countries. Dr. Rosana Richtmann, director of the Infection Control Committee (ICC), Santa Joana Hospital and Maternity, São Paulo, Brazil, former president of the São Paulo Society of Infectious Diseases, said that Brazil has implemented dengue vaccination in its public health system since 2024, starting in 521 municipalities and expanding to all 2,752 municipalities, with 24 million doses distributed. "Real-world data from São Paulo during 2024–2025 show that a two-dose schedule reduced the risk of symptomatic dengue by 73.1 per cent and the risk of hospitalization by 87.9 per cent. Protection was sustained despite the re-emergence of DENV-3. In Indonesia, dengue vaccination is also being implemented alongside health technology solutions to strengthen proactive prevention in high-risk areas," she said. The draft 2026 National Guidelines for Dengue Diagnosis and Treatment, presented at the summit by the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, introduced key updates to the prevention chapter. The draft underscores the importance of dengue prevention, particularly in the absence of a specific antiviral treatment. It recommends a comprehensive approach that combines dengue vaccination in accordance with current regulations with surveillance activities, the MoH recommended preventive measures, and vector control interventions such as bite prevention and elimination of mosquito breeding sites. The coordinated use of proactive prevention measures is seen as a policy signal aligned with WHO recommendations for an integrated dengue control strategy. To translate scientific advances into practice, coordination among regulatory agencies, the medical community, and healthcare partners is essential. As a scientific partner for the second consecutive year, Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Vietnam supports efforts to boost evidence-based prevention solutions and raise community awareness about dengue. Benjamin Ping, country head, Takeda Vietnam, said that whilst the awareness of dengue in Vietnam was relatively high, research shows that most people in Vietnam do not fully understand the risks, severity and urgency associated with dengue to themselves and their families. More proactive preventive action is needed to reduce the burden of Dengue in Vietnam. “Takeda is working alongside international partners and health authorities to support evidence-based prevention solutions aimed at protecting public health including the use of vaccination as part of an integrated prevention and control strategy," he said. With dengue occurring year-round, experts at the summit called for coordinated implementation of proactive prevention measures at all levels - from strengthening epidemiological surveillance and treatment capacity to behaviour change and encouraging appropriate vaccination. The vaccine currently available in Vietnam is the first and only dengue vaccine approved by the MoH. The vaccine is also recommended by WHO for use in countries with a high dengue burden and has received WHO prequalification for quality, safety, and efficacy. To date, the vaccine has been approved in 43 countries, with over 32 million doses distributed globally, and has been integrated into public immunisation programmes in Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, Indonesia, Honduras, Paraguay, Peru, and Thailand. content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Dengue fever can worsen; be vigilant during the fever-reducing phase. Many dengue fever patients require emergency treatment with severely low platelet counts, liver damage, and blood clotting disorders, even though they were previously perfectly healthy. Báo Hải Phòng•11/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Hai Duong ward sprays chemicals to kill the source of dengue fever. Photo: THANH HOA Many patients developed severe symptoms. The National Hospital for Tropical Diseases has recently received and treated many severe cases of dengue fever, including patients with serious liver damage, drastically reduced platelet count, and blood clotting disorders. A typical case is Mrs. BH (53 years old, from Hai Phong ), who was hospitalized after 5 days of continuous high fever of 39-40 degrees Celsius, accompanied by general body aches, nausea, frequent vomiting, and abdominal pain. Previously, the patient had self-medicated with paracetamol at home to reduce fever but without improvement. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Test results from a nearby medical facility confirmed that Ms. H. had dengue fever, with her platelet count rapidly dropping from 38 to 21 G/L, and her liver enzymes elevated. Due to the worsening condition, she was transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Upon admission, the patient still had a high fever, severe pain in the right lower rib area, and petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) under the skin. Platelet count was only 23 G/L, accompanied by coagulation disorders. Doctors diagnosed the patient with severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever with liver damage, requiring close monitoring for the risk of bleeding, circulatory disorders, and complications. Another case is Ms. PL (23 years old, from Hanoi ), who was previously completely healthy but also developed severe symptoms after contracting dengue fever. The patient experienced high fevers up to 39 degrees Celsius, chills, headache, body aches, abdominal pain, nausea, frequent vomiting, and diarrhea. After receiving treatment at a local medical facility without improvement, and with continued unfavorable test results including a significant drop in platelets and elevated liver enzymes, she was referred to a higher-level facility. At the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, ultrasound results revealed fluid in the abdominal cavity and bilateral pleural spaces. This is indicative of plasma leakage, a crucial mechanism that can worsen dengue fever, potentially leading to decreased circulating volume, hemodynamic instability, and shock if not detected and treated promptly. The patient was also assessed to have severe liver damage. You may also like Currently, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is treating 16 dengue fever patients, many of whom are in serious condition and require intensive monitoring and treatment. Just because the fever has gone down doesn't mean the illness is out of danger. Patients with dengue fever are being treated at Hai Duong Tropical Diseases Hospital. Photo: THANH HOA According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the two severe cases mentioned above both had significantly reduced platelet counts, elevated liver enzymes, blood clotting disorders, and many other warning signs. These abnormalities indicate that the disease has progressed seriously, requiring close monitoring to promptly detect and manage complications. According to Dr. Phuc, a notable characteristic of dengue fever is that the disease can worsen precisely when the patient's fever begins to subside. The dangerous phase usually occurs between the 3rd and 7th day after onset. At this time, the patient is at risk of plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or organ damage. If not detected and treated promptly, severe plasma leakage can cause hypovolemia, shock, multiple organ failure, and be life-threatening. Therefore, patients and their families should not assess the severity of the illness based solely on body temperature. The absence of fever does not mean the illness is cured or has passed the critical stage. Dr. Pham Van Phuc also noted that thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) is a common symptom in dengue fever patients, but this indicator alone cannot be used to assess the severity. Doctors need to consider the overall clinical condition, signs of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and signs of organ damage to determine the risk of complications. People who have or suspect they have dengue fever should go to a medical facility immediately if they experience warning signs such as severe or persistent abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, lethargy or restlessness, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, decreased urination, cold hands and feet, and extreme fatigue. For cases where doctors instruct patients to monitor and treat themselves at home, they need to rest, drink plenty of fluids, and regularly monitor their temperature, appetite, urine output, and any unusual symptoms. Do not increase the dosage of fever-reducing medication or use anti-inflammatory drugs without a prescription, as some medications can increase the risk of bleeding. You may also like In particular, patients need to attend follow-up appointments as scheduled, undergo tests as prescribed, and be closely monitored from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness. This is a crucial period for early detection of the risk of worsening condition, even when external symptoms seem to subside. Dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the Dengue virus, transmitted primarily through Aedes mosquitoes, and can affect people of all ages, including those who were previously healthy. To prevent the disease, people need to proactively eliminate stagnant water sources, kill mosquito larvae, reduce mosquito bites, and maintain a clean living environment. Vaccination against dengue fever is also a proactive preventive measure, and should be done according to the instructions of healthcare workers and the regulations of the vaccination facility. However, vaccines do not replace mosquito control measures and prevention of mosquito bites. If dengue fever symptoms are suspected, people should still go to a medical facility for examination, testing, and appropriate monitoring guidance. content_title: Information regarding two cases of dengue fever with very complicated developments.
content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Information regarding two cases of dengue fever with very complicated developments. The moment a patient's temperature begins to drop after several days of continuous high fever often creates a false sense of security, leading them to believe the illness has subsided. However, according to medical experts, this is actually the most dangerous stage of dengue fever, posing a risk of massive bleeding, shock, and serious organ damage. Hà Nội Mới•11/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Critically ill despite being in perfectly good health beforehand. On the afternoon of November 11th, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases announced that it had recently admitted and treated two cases of dengue fever with very complicated developments. Notably, both patients had previously been in normal health and had no recorded chronic underlying medical conditions. The first case involves a 53-year-old female patient, BH, residing in Hai Phong, who had never had dengue fever. Approximately five days before being transferred to the hospital, she experienced a continuous high fever of 39-40°C, accompanied by fatigue, nausea, frequent vomiting, and abdominal cramps. After self-medicating with fever-reducing medication at home without success, she sought medical attention at a local health facility and was diagnosed with dengue fever. Alarmingly, her platelet count dropped sharply and rapidly from 38 G/L to 21 G/L, and her liver enzymes surged, necessitating an urgent transfer to a higher-level hospital. Closely monitor the patient's condition. Photo: Thanh Nguyen At the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the patient was still experiencing high fever, severe pain in the right lower rib area, and petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) under the skin at the injection sites. Advanced laboratory tests revealed a platelet count of only 23 G/L, a sharp increase in AST to 1,939 U/L, and ALT to 804 U/L, along with severe coagulation disorders. The patient was diagnosed with severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever with acute liver damage and a risk of circulatory complications. Another case involves a 23-year-old female patient, PL, residing in Hanoi . Her illness began approximately 7 days prior with symptoms including intermittent high fever, chills, severe headache, general body aches, and digestive disorders. After monitoring at a medical facility, her condition not only failed to improve but also worsened: her platelet count dropped to 21 G/L, AST liver enzymes reached 1,907 U/L, and ALT was at 883 U/L. The patient's condition is developing in a very complicated way. Photo: Thanh Nguyen Specifically, the ultrasound results revealed bilateral pleural effusion and ascites. This is clear evidence of plasma leakage – a key pathogenesis that causes a rapid decrease in intravascular volume, pushing the patient into circulatory shock and multiple organ failure if not treated promptly. You may also like A fever reduction might lead people to believe they're recovered. According to MSc. Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit (National Hospital for Tropical Diseases), dengue fever is caused by a virus transmitted primarily through Aedes mosquitoes, can attack anyone, and can be severe at any age. Dr. Phuc noted that, in reality, many people only pay attention to platelet count or body temperature to estimate the severity of the disease. However, low platelet count is only one of the criteria. Assessing the severity requires a comprehensive consideration of clinical signs: blood concentration level, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, mucosal bleeding, and the function of internal organs. Dengue fever often worsens precisely when the patient begins to recover from a fever. Photo: Thanh Nguyen "In both cases, in addition to extremely low platelet counts, the patients also suffered severe liver damage and blood clotting disorders. This is a clear warning that the disease has entered a dangerous stage and requires close, hourly monitoring in the intensive care unit," Dr. Phuc emphasized. The key point highlighted by experts is that dengue fever often worsens precisely when the patient's fever begins to subside, which is between the 3rd and 7th day of the onset of the disease. This is when the inflammatory response in blood vessels increases, causing plasma to leak into the interstitial space, leading to blood concentration, hypotension, and the risk of internal bleeding. Neglecting follow-up care and examinations once the patient's fever has subsided is a disastrous mistake. Monitor your health proactively and avoid self-medicating. Doctors advise that people with or suspected of having dengue fever who are being treated at home should strictly follow medical guidelines: get adequate rest, and replenish fluids orally (oral rehydration solution, coconut water, fruit juice). You may also like Absolutely do not increase the dosage of Paracetamol on your own to avoid poisoning and increased burden on liver cells. In particular, people should not use non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as Aspirin, Ibuprofen, as they inhibit platelet aggregation, increasing the risk of difficult-to-control gastrointestinal bleeding. Patients and their families should go to the hospital immediately if they notice any of the following warning signs: Pain or discomfort in the liver area or severe, persistent abdominal pain; Nausea and frequent vomiting; Bleeding: bleeding gums, nosebleeds, black stools, or vomiting dark-colored fluid; A lethargic, drowsy, restless, and agitated state of mind; Symptoms include a significant decrease in urine output (oliguria), cold extremities, bluish discoloration of the skin, or extreme fatigue. To protect yourself and the community, the most fundamental measure remains controlling disease vectors: Actively maintaining a clean living environment, covering water containers tightly, removing stagnant water to eliminate mosquito larvae, and maintaining the habit of sleeping under mosquito nets. In addition, people can consult with preventive health facilities about vaccination to proactively minimize the risk of contracting the disease and experiencing severe symptoms. X Culture - Entertainment Culture Entertainment Fashion Nice book Real estate Nice house Zoning Education Education policy Enrollment Marriage and family Family stories Love 360 Rasing child Technology Digital world Wepon - Military Car Car market Driving safe Employment News Labor consulting Labor export 59s Latest News Health Medical - Nutrition - Beautify - Diseases Dengue fever reinfection 3 times, be wary of the risk of severe progression Hạnh Thơm - 10:44, Tue Nov 10, 2026 (GMT+7) Hanoi - People who have had dengue fever are still at risk of re-infection. Notably, subsequent infections can progress severely, especially in people with underlying diseases. People who have had dengue fever are still at risk of getting it back many times. In particular, the disease can develop complicatedly, causing dangerous complications if not monitored and treated promptly. Photo: Hanh Thom At the Infectious Diseases Unit, Department of Occupational Diseases, Thanh Nhan Hospital, a 47-year-old male patient (Hanoi) was diagnosed with dengue fever after two days of symptoms of headache, high fever of 38-39 degrees Celsius and fatigue. Before being admitted to the hospital, the patient had symptoms of dizziness and fainting at home. This is the third time I have dengue fever. However, in this case I feel more tired, prolonged headache and thrombocytopenia. I have not been vaccinated against dengue fever. After this treatment, I actively vaccinated myself," the male patient said. Doctors examine patients with dengue fever with platelet hypoplasia. Photo: Hanh Thom In another case, a 20-year-old male patient (Hanoi), was admitted to the hospital in a state of high fever of 40 degrees Celsius, headache and many rashes on the skin. Recognizing abnormal signs, the family took the patient to the hospital for examination. After 11 days of treatment, the dengue fever condition has subsided, but liver enzymes are still increasing, so the patient continues to be monitored, not yet eligible for discharge. The patient could not identify the source of infection. According to BSCKII Nguyen Thu Huong, Head of the Infectious Diseases Unit, Department of Occupational Diseases, Thanh Nhan Hospital, the unit is currently treating about 20 dengue fever patients. Compared to previous years, the number of cases tends to decrease, and no sudden increase has been recorded. However, compared to the same period last year, the number of dengue fever patients at this time is higher. Because the department receives many groups of infectious diseases, prioritizing respiratory diseases, dengue fever patients are treated in many specialties depending on the severity. At the Infectious Diseases Unit alone, the unit receives about 4-5 dengue fever patients per day, including cases with severe progression. BSCKII Nguyen Thu Huong, Head of Infectious Diseases Unit, Department of Occupational Diseases, Thanh Nhan Hospital. Photo: Hanh Thom Notably, Dr. Huong said that the unit had previously received a patient with dengue fever on the fourth day, who also had a history of idiopathic thrombocytopenia and was maintaining corticosteroid treatment at a dose of about 40 mg/day. At the time of admission, the patient's platelet count was about 130,000/μl. However, after only two days, this index dropped sharply to about 1,000/μl, making the condition particularly serious. According to the doctor, this is a case at high risk due to dengue fever appearing on the background of idiopathic thrombocytopenia. Doctors recommend that people should not be subjective when symptoms of high fever, headache, fatigue or rash appear. When suspected of having dengue fever, it is necessary to go to a medical facility for examination, testing and appropriate monitoring instructions. In particular, people with underlying medical conditions need to fully inform their medical history and medications they are using so that doctors can assess risks and have timely treatment plans. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 12, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Red Microalga Expresses Dengue Structural Antigens Across All Four Serotypes by November 7, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Red Microalga Expresses Dengue Structural Antigens Across All Four Serotypes Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have achieved the heterologous expression of recombinant dengue virus capsid–premembrane–envelope (C-prM-E) structural antigen constructs representing all four serotypes (DV1–DV4) in the red microalga Porphyridium purpureum. The demonstration establishes a microalgal expression platform aimed at supporting the development of plant-derived dengue vaccine candidates. The dengue virus remains a significant global health threat, while existing vaccines continue to raise concerns regarding safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness. Microalgae offer an alternative approach for producing non-naturally occurring proteins, supported by their Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) status, straightforward scalability, and capacity to perform eukaryotic post-translational modifications. To generate the antigens, gene constructs containing capsid–premembrane–envelope polyprotein fragments with C-terminal epitope tags were cloned into pCAMBIA1301 vectors. The vectors were subsequently introduced into P. purpureum using Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology Read Med Journals Identify Plants Study Marine Life Chromosomal integration of all four serotype constructs was confirmed via polymerase chain reaction amplification, which produced the expected 2.5-kilobase amplicons. Subsequent SDS-PAGE analysis identified protein bands at approximately 85 kDa, matching the predicted molecular weight of the processed CprME-derived proteins. Western blot assays using anti-DENV-2 and anti-FLAG antibodies verified that the recombinant antigens were identical and exhibited immune system reactivity across all four serotypes. These findings indicate that P. purpureum provides an effective production system that may facilitate scalable manufacturing of tetravalent dengue vaccines, especially in resource-limited regions where the virus is prevalent. In the study, the researchers cloned gene constructs containing capsid-premembrane-envelope polyprotein fragments with C-terminal epitope tags into pCAMBIA1301 vectors, using Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation to introduce them into Porphyridium purpureum. Polymerase chain reaction amplification confirmed chromosomal integration across all four serotypes by yielding the expected 2.5-kilobase amplicons. Protein evaluation using SDS-PAGE identified bands at approximately 85 kDa, matching the predicted molecular weight of the processed structural proteins. Subsequent western blot assays using anti-DENV-2 and anti-FLAG antibodies confirmed that the recombinant antigens reacted with the immune system across all four serotypes, supporting the platform’s potential for producing plant-derived tetravalent dengue vaccine candidates in resource-limited settings. Discover more Meet Dietitians Vaccine vaccines Find Vaccines vaccine The global health burden imposed by the dengue virus is compounded by limitations associated with current vaccine options, which exhibit notable shortcomings regarding safety, protective efficacy, and overall cost-effectiveness. In response to these constraints, microalgal production hosts offer an alternative strategy for generating non-naturally occurring recombinant proteins. Organisms such as the red microalga Porphyridium purpureum combine several advantageous manufacturing properties, including a Generally Recognized As Safe designation, straightforward cultivation scalability, and the eukaryotic cellular machinery necessary to carry out complex post-translational modifications on synthesized viral antigens. To establish expression across the entire antigenic breadth of the virus, recombinant constructs were engineered to encompass the capsid, premembrane, and envelope structural polyprotein domains for all four dengue virus serotypes, designated DV1 through DV4. Each polyprotein gene fragment incorporated a C-terminal epitope tag to aid characterization before insertion into pCAMBIA1301 expression vectors. Delivery into Porphyridium purpureum host cells was then mediated through Agrobacterium tumefaciens transformation, introducing the recombinant viral cassettes into the microalga. Molecular validation confirmed stable genomic incorporation across every target serotype. Polymerase chain reaction analysis successfully amplified the expected 2.5-kilobase DNA products, demonstrating that the structural gene sequences had integrated into the host microalga chromosomes. Electrophoretic assessment via sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis revealed protein bands resolving near 85 kilodaltons. This observed migration aligned with the predicted theoretical mass for the processed capsid-premembrane-envelope recombinant proteins, indicating that the algal cells appropriately synthesized the engineered viral antigens. To establish antigenic properties and identity, investigators performed immunoblot testing utilizing both anti-FLAG and anti-DENV-2 antibodies. The western blot analyses confirmed that the recombinant proteins produced across all four serotypes reacted with the immune reagents and displayed structural uniformity. By demonstrating robust expression and immune system interactivity for DV1, DV2, DV3, and DV4, the research highlights P. purpureum as a viable microalgal host for manufacturing cost-effective, plant-derived vaccine candidates. This platform holds particular promise for enabling scalable, large-scale production of tetravalent formulations to serve dengue-endemic areas facing substantial economic and healthcare resource constraints. content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Several children are in critical condition due to dengue fever, requiring dialysis and mechanical ventilation. (Dan Tri Newspaper) - Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City has continuously saved the lives of many children with critical dengue fever, severe complications, and requiring ECMO and continuous blood dialysis. Find Family Lawyer Báo Dân trí•06/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Recently, the Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City admitted a 27-month-old female child, LMH, from Thanh Hoa province, with dengue fever. She was hospitalized with a continuous high fever, vomiting, and lethargy. Critically ill children require dialysis and ECMO treatment. According to the medical history, the child fell ill 3 days prior, experiencing a continuous high fever and vomiting approximately 3 times a day. The family self-medicated the child with unknown drugs. Subsequently, the child became lethargic and was taken to the City Children's Hospital, where they were admitted to the Infectious Diseases Department for treatment. The antigen test results were positive for the Dengue virus. However, just 12 hours after admission, the child suddenly developed respiratory failure, cyanosis, mottled skin, and a drop in blood pressure. Doctors had to resuscitate the child with intravenous fluids and vasopressors. Due to the progressive respiratory failure, the patient was intubated, placed on a ventilator, and given high doses of vasopressors. Find Family Lawyer The child was diagnosed with fulminant myocarditis and cardiogenic shock on the third day due to Dengue hemorrhagic fever, along with liver damage, and was transferred to the Intensive Care and Toxicology Unit. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Find Family Lawyer Here, the child was lethargic, with pale lips, requiring mechanical ventilation, had cold extremities, a prolonged capillary refill time of 4-5 seconds, and a weak radial pulse. Heart rate was increased, blood pressure was decreased, and echocardiography showed a continued decrease in ejection fraction (EF). Given the critical condition, doctors implemented intensive resuscitation with various vasopressors, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and consulted with the ECMO team. Find Treatments The child was placed on a VA ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) system, connected via the right internal jugular artery and vein. A 27-month-old child is in critical condition due to dengue fever (Photo: Provided by the hospital). During treatment, the child continued to develop complications including multiple organ failure and severe liver and kidney damage. Doctors had to combine 8 consecutive hemodialysis sessions, blood transfusions, platelet transfusions, electrolyte and acid-base balance adjustments, and medication to support liver function. Find Family Lawyer You may also like After nearly 5 weeks on ECMO along with intensive care, continuous hemodialysis, and organ support, the child's cardiac function gradually recovered. Ejection fraction (EF) improved to 48-52%, and blood pressure stabilized during the ECMO weaning test. The child was weaned off ECMO, the vascular cannula were removed, then weaned off the ventilator, switched to oxygen via cannula, and then breathed ambient air spontaneously. The heart rate returned to a normal sinus rhythm, liver and kidney function recovered, and the child urinated adequately. After nearly two months of treatment, the child's health has improved significantly. Find Family Lawyer According to doctors, this is a rare case of myocarditis and cardiogenic shock in a child with dengue fever. There are currently no precise figures on the frequency of this complication, as most of the medical literature only records cases from case reports and small case series. Globally , only a few cases of myocarditis and cardiogenic shock due to dengue fever in children have been treated with VA ECMO. Warning signs of dengue fever worsening in children. Also at the City Children's Hospital, doctors recently saved the life of a 17-day-old infant suffering from dengue shock, blood clotting disorders, and severe liver damage. A 17-day-old infant is in shock due to dengue fever (Photo: Provided by the hospital). The patient is a boy residing in Ho Chi Minh City. Before being admitted to the hospital, the child had a moderate, intermittent high fever for two days, exhibited startled reactions during sleep, and had a red rash on his skin. Test results showed decreased platelet count and positive dengue antigen. The child was diagnosed with dengue fever on the second day, treated with fever reducers, and continued breastfeeding. By the third day, the child's condition worsened; they became lethargic, irritable, had a weak radial pulse, cold extremities, and their blood pressure dropped to 60/40 mmHg. Petechiae appeared on the hands, feet, and abdomen, along with mottled skin. Laboratory tests revealed an increase in hematocrit to 45%, decreased platelets, and elevated liver enzymes. Doctors diagnosed the child with dengue hemorrhagic shock and severe liver damage and immediately initiated intensive shock treatment according to protocol. You may also like Because the patient was so young, establishing an IV line proved difficult, and the child developed bruising at multiple injection sites. The doctors continued to administer anti-shock fluids using a high-molecular-weight solution. Test results revealed severe coagulation dysfunction. The child received blood transfusions, platelet concentrates, and albumin to support shock management. Additionally, the child received liver support, respiratory support with oxygen, and CPAP ventilation. After 72 hours of treatment, the child's hemodynamic status and liver damage improved. The patient showed no further signs of bleeding, was alert, feeding well, and urinating adequately. Based on the above cases, doctors advise parents not to be complacent when children contract dengue fever, especially in the early days when the disease can progress rapidly and dangerous complications can appear. To prevent the disease, people need to actively eliminate mosquitoes and larvae, sleep under mosquito nets, and proactively monitor children's health. In addition to preventive measures, a dengue fever vaccine is now available for children aged 4 and older, with a schedule of two doses administered 3 months apart. Parents can take their children to vaccination centers for advice on the appropriate indications and vaccination schedule. Signs that indicate a child needs immediate medical attention. If a child has a high fever for more than two days and exhibits any of the following signs, they should be taken to a medical facility immediately: fussiness, restlessness, tossing and turning, or lethargy; abdominal pain; nosebleeds, bleeding gums, vomiting blood, or passing black stools; cold hands and feet, lying still and not playing, refusing to breastfeed or eat. Standing water creates ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes, raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including dengue fever. The Florida Department of Health reports nearly 300 dengue cases statewide this year. However, there are currently no reported cases in Broward County for November. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted through the bite of an infected mosquito. Health officials say the illness is typically more prevalent during Florida's rainy season, and recent flooding could create conditions that increase the risk of transmission. Dr. Craig Harrison of Broward Health Medical Center says residents should be aware of the symptoms, which can include fever, body aches, and headaches, particularly pain behind the eyes. In more severe cases, patients may develop a rash or experience bleeding. Nausea and vomiting are also possible symptoms. Meanwhile, the City of Davie says it has already begun mosquito spraying and is investigating whether additional ground or aerial spraying operations may be necessary. The flooding has also forced several parks to close, including Oak Hill Equestrian Park, as crews continue to address the effects of days of heavy rain. The recent downpours caused widespread disruptions across Broward County, including school closures, flooded homes, and stranded vehicles. content_title: Dengue fever is on the rise, and doctors warn of the most critical period.
content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Dengue fever is on the rise, and doctors warn of the most critical period. Nationwide, more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever have been recorded, with 21 deaths. Doctors warn of the dangerous phase when the fever begins to subside. Check Symptoms Báo Gia đình và Xã hội•07/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 According to statistics from the Ministry of Health , in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. Meanwhile, the same period in 2025 recorded approximately 106,000 cases. In Ho Chi Minh City, according to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), in week 44 (from October 26 to November 1), the city recorded 1,959 cases of dengue fever, an increase of 16.2% compared to the average of the previous four weeks. From the beginning of the year to the end of week 44, Ho Chi Minh City has recorded 44,549 cases. 17-day-old infant in severe dengue shock. Recently, the Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City admitted and treated a 17-day-old boy from Tan Vinh Loc commune who suffered from dengue shock with many dangerous complications. A 17-day-old infant suffering from dengue shock is being treated at the City Children's Hospital. Photo: Provided by the hospital. Reportedly, the child's mother also had dengue fever and was treated at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases. After the mother was discharged, the child began to develop a fever. Check Symptoms According to the medical history, the child had a moderate, intermittent fever for two days, accompanied by startling during sleep and a red rash on the skin. Laboratory results showed a significant decrease in platelets, and the NS1 antigen test was positive for Dengue virus. By the third day, the child's condition worsened, exhibiting lethargy, fussiness, weak pulse, cold extremities, blood pressure dropping to 60/40 mmHg, and numerous petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) on the skin. Laboratory tests showed a continued decrease in platelet count to 24,000/mm3, and elevated liver enzymes. Doctors diagnosed the child with dengue hemorrhagic shock, severe liver damage, and coagulation disorders. The patient received intensive shock treatment, including fluid resuscitation, blood transfusions, platelet concentrates, and albumin, while also supporting liver and respiratory function. Due to the child's young age, establishing an intravenous line proved difficult. During treatment, the child developed bruising at the injection site, vomited dark brown fluid, and exhibited unstable hemodynamics. You may also like After 72 hours of intensive treatment, the child's hemodynamic status and liver damage gradually improved, with no further signs of bleeding, and the child was alert, feeding, and urinating well. Dr. Nguyen Minh Tien, Deputy Director of the City Children's Hospital, said that dengue fever can occur in newborns, but the symptoms are sometimes atypical and easily confused with sepsis or other diseases. Check Symptoms Patients being treated for dengue fever at the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Photo: DH. Check Symptoms Dengue hemorrhagic shock in this age group is uncommon and may be related to plasma leakage, myocardial failure, or sepsis. Therefore, when infants show signs of fever or other health abnormalities, families should take them to a medical facility with a neonatal specialist for examination, diagnosis of the cause, and timely treatment. The absence of fever does not mean the illness is cured. According to Dr. Nguyen Huu Tri, a specialist in the Emergency Department at Children's Hospital 2, dengue fever typically progresses through three stages: the fever stage, the critical stage, and the recovery stage. The critical stage usually occurs from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, especially on the 4th or 5th day, when the child's fever begins to subside or disappears. According to Dr. Nguyen Huu Tri, the period after the fever subsides is when patients are at risk of plasma leakage, leading to shock, multi-organ damage, and even death if not detected and treated promptly. Dr. Tri noted that test results need to be evaluated daily and combined with clinical manifestations. In the early days, blood counts may not change significantly, while platelet counts gradually decrease as the disease progresses. Therefore, children with dengue fever need to be closely monitored from the very first days of the illness, and should have follow-up appointments as directed by their doctor, especially during the critical phase. Not only children, but adults are also at risk of developing severe symptoms when they contract dengue fever. You may also like Dr. Nguyen Thanh Phong, Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases, said that in the last 10 years, adults have accounted for a large proportion of dengue fever cases, possibly more than two-thirds. However, many people are still complacent, believing that dengue fever is not dangerous or that the absence of fever means recovery. In reality, many patients are admitted to the hospital when they have already developed severe shock, heavy bleeding, or multiple organ failure. Dr. Nguyen Thanh Phong, a specialist in internal medicine, warns that when experiencing a high fever for three consecutive days, people should consider the possibility of dengue fever and seek medical attention for examination, testing, and appropriate treatment. In particular, if symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lethargy, extreme fatigue, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath, unusual bleeding, or decreased urination appear, patients should be taken to a medical facility immediately, even if the fever has subsided. Doctors advise that people suspected of having dengue fever should stay well-hydrated, use oral rehydration solution (ORS) as directed by healthcare professionals, eat soft, easily digestible foods, and get adequate rest. They should absolutely not self-medicate with ibuprofen, aspirin, or other anti-inflammatory pain relievers due to the risk of increased bleeding. Furthermore, they should not attempt to administer intravenous fluids at home. According to the Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases, self-administering intravenous fluids when suffering from dengue fever poses many risks. Intravenous fluids administered at the wrong time or with incorrect indications can cause complications and make the process of combating shock more difficult. To prevent the disease, people need to proactively eliminate mosquitoes and larvae, remove objects that hold stagnant water, and avoid mosquito bites. content: Rescuers save 17-day-old newborn boy suffering from dengue shock and severe liver damage. On the evening of November 6th, the City Children's Hospital announced that it had successfully treated a case of dengue shock in a 17-day-old infant, accompanied by severe liver damage, coagulation disorders, and severe thrombocytopenia. Check Symptoms Báo Sài Gòn Giải phóng • 06/11/2026 The child is receiving intensive treatment at the City Children's Hospital (Photo: Provided by the hospital). Discover more Find Treatments Shop Baby Gear Track Pregnancy The patient is a young boy residing in Tan Vinh Loc ward, Ho Chi Minh City, who was admitted to the hospital after two days of intermittent fever, startling awake during sleep, and a red rash on his skin. Test results showed the child was positive for the Dengue virus, and his platelet count had dropped to 47,000/mm3. By the third day of the illness, the child's condition suddenly worsened, becoming lethargic, irritable, with cold hands and feet, low blood pressure, and numerous petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) on the skin. Tests showed a continued sharp drop in platelet count and elevated liver enzymes. Doctors diagnosed the child with dengue hemorrhagic shock, severe liver damage, and a coagulation disorder. Check Symptoms You may also like Ho Chi Minh City: Newborn baby saved from severe dengue shock. When infants show signs of fever or other health abnormalities, families should take them to a medical facility with a neonatal specialist for examination, testing, and determination of the cause. Saving the life of a newborn suffering from severe dengue shock. A 17-day-old boy with severe complications from dengue fever has been successfully treated by doctors at Ho Chi Minh City Children's Hospital. Doctors advise parents not to underestimate dengue fever, especially in children. Saving the life of a 17-day-old infant suffering from dengue shock and severe liver damage. Doctors at the Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City have successfully saved a 17-day-old infant suffering from dengue shock, blood clotting disorders, and severe liver damage. The child received intensive shock treatment, including fluid resuscitation, blood transfusions, platelet concentrate, albumin, and support for liver and respiratory function. After 72 hours of treatment, hemodynamic status and liver damage improved, and the child was alert, feeding, and urinating adequately. Before the child fell ill, the mother also contracted dengue fever and was treated at the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases. According to Dr. Nguyen Minh Tien, Deputy Director of the City Children's Hospital, dengue fever in newborns can present with atypical symptoms, easily mistaken for sepsis or other illnesses. Although dengue shock is uncommon at this age, the disease still carries the risk of serious complications. "When infants show signs of fever or other health abnormalities, families should quickly take them to a medical facility with a neonatal specialist for examination, diagnosis, and timely treatment," advised Dr. Nguyen Minh Tien. Check Symptoms You may also like 17-day-old infant suffers from dengue shock and severe liver damage. (Dan Tri Newspaper) - At just 17 days old, a baby boy in Ho Chi Minh City has fallen into a state of dengue shock, blood clotting disorder, severe liver damage, and is in critical condition. Warning of severe dengue fever in overweight children. VTV.vn - A 12-year-old boy is suffering from dengue shock accompanied by gastrointestinal bleeding, liver damage, and critical respiratory failure. Doctors warn that early recognition of severe symptoms is crucial for timely emergency treatment. A 50 kg boy is in critical condition, with liver enzymes soaring to over 3,000 U/L after 4 days of fever. After three days of high fever, the 12-year-old boy suddenly experienced abdominal pain, vomited brown fluid, had black stools, and then went into dengue shock, respiratory failure, and severe liver damage. According to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control, from October 26th to November 1st, 2026 (week 44), the city recorded 1,959 cases of dengue fever, an increase of 16.2% compared to the average of the previous four weeks. The total number of dengue fever cases accumulated from the beginning of 2026 to week 44 is 44,549. Communes and wards with a high number of dengue fever cases per 100,000 people include Con Dao Special Zone, Ngai Giao, and Minh Thanh.
